newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong extends condolences on Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong extends condolences on Deng's death.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten extended condolences on Thursday on the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping and the territory's top civil servant said she did not expect his death to affect Hong Kong's transition to China.

Television and radio suspended normal programming to devote the airways to biographies, analyses and retrospectives of the life of the man regarded as the architect of Hong Kong's impending reunion with China.
Chris Patten, the 28th and last British Governor of Hong Kong, described Deng as an historic figure.
"I learned with regret this morning of the death of Mr Deng Xiaoping," Patten said in a statement.

"He will be regarded by future generations as an historic figure. His concept of "one country, two systems" helped to make possible the successful negotiation of the Joint Declaration, and thus to lay the foundation for Hong Kong's stability and prosperity after 1997," Patten said.
The Joint Declaration is the treaty which governs the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule.

China has promised Hong Kong considerable autonomy under Deng's principle of one country, two systems. It will permit its capitalist way of life remain and has promised the people of Hong Kong will run the territory of six million.
Patten's deputy Anson Chan, who will serve as deputy to Hong Kong's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, also expressed her regret.
"I would just like to say that I learned with deep regret the passing of Mr Deng Xiaoping.
"I would just like to represent and say on behalf of the entire Hong Kong civil service we send our deepest condolences to Mr Deng's family."
Chan said she did not expect Deng's death to affect Hong Kong's transition to China.
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said he did not expect Deng's death to have much of an adverse effect on the markets.
"The Hong Kong markets and the Chinese markets have prepared for this moment. I do not think there would be very major volatility," Tsang, Hong Kong's top economic planner, told reporters.
"Hong Kong is a very strong financial centre... any slight impact would surely pass quickly."
"Deng Xiaoping contributed very much to China's economic opening up ... and I feel great sorrow like all Hong Kong people.
Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, was visiting Beijing when Deng died. He had been expected to report to China's leadership on his choice of key post-handover officials.
